'''''Cylindropuntia imbricata''''', the '''cane cholla''' ('''walking stick cholla''', '''tree cholla''', or '''chainlink cactus'''), is a [[cactus]] found in the [[Southwestern United States]] and northern [[Mexico]], including some cooler regions in comparison to many other cacti. It occurs primarily in the arid regions of the Southwestern United States in the states of [[Kansas]],<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|242415157|Cylindropuntia imbricata|first=Donald J.|last=Pinkava|volume=4}}</ref> [[Oklahoma]], [[Texas]], [[New Mexico]], [[Arizona]], [[Colorado]], and [[Nevada]]. It is often conspicuous because of its shrubby or even tree-like size, its silhouette, and its long-lasting yellowish fruits.

==Distribution and habitat==
The cane cholla's range is the arid regions of [[Nevada]], [[Arizona]], [[New Mexico]], [[Colorado]], [[Oklahoma]], [[Kansas]], and [[Texas]], south to [[Durango]], [[Zacatecas]], and [[San Luis Potosí]].<ref name = ars>{{GRIN | access-date = 2007-03-13}}</ref> It occurs at altitudes from {{convert|1200|to|2300|m|ft|abbr=on}} and is hardy for a cactus ([[USDA plant hardiness zone|USDA Zone]] 5A).<ref name=Horticopia>{{cite web | title = ''Opuntia imbricata'' Chainlink Cactus | work = Garden Plants List | publisher = Horticopia, Inc. | year = 2004 | url = http://www.aboutgardenplants.com/Opuntia_imbricata.shtml | access-date = 2006-07-17 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20061106165150/http://www.aboutgardenplants.com/Opuntia_imbricata.shtml | archive-date = 2006-11-06 }}</ref>

In parts of its range, often just below the [[pinyon pine|pinyon]]-[[juniper]] belt, it can be abundant, surrounded by low [[Graminoid|grasses]] and [[forb]]s that are brown most of the year; in such places chollas are conspicuous since they are the only tall and green plant. Plants may form [[Thicket|thickets]] or be spaced at a few times their width in "gardens".
[[File:Cylindropuntia imbricata P1010574.jpg|thumb|left|invasive [[Kwiambal National Park|Kwiambal NP]], NSW, Australia]]
This species is a noxious [[Invasive species|invasive]] in Australia in old mining localities and along watercourses. It is known there by the common names of Devil's rope cactus or Devil's rope pear.<ref name="Weeds Australia">{{cite web|title=Devil's Rope Cactus|work=Weeds Australia|publisher=Australian Weeds Committee|url=http://www.weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=S52|access-date=21 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130413145758/http://weeds.org.au/cgi-bin/weedident.cgi?tpl=plant.tpl&state=&s=&ibra=all&card=S52|archive-date=13 April 2013}}</ref><ref name=APNI/> It is a declared [[noxious weed]] in [[New South Wales]] and also occurs in [[Queensland]], [[Northern Territory]], [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], and [[South Australia]].<ref name="Weeds Australia"/><ref name=APNI>{{cite web |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/cgi-bin/apni?TAXON_NAME=Cylindropuntia+imbricata|title=''Cylindropuntia imbricata'' |access-date=21 May 2012 |work= [[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI), IBIS database|publisher = Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, Australian Government, Canberra}}</ref><ref name=NSW>{{cite web |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Cylindropuntia~imbricata |title=''Cylindropuntia imbricata'' (Engelm.) F.M.Knuth |access-date=21 May 2012 |work= PlantNET - New South Wales Flora Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens & Domain Trust, Sydney Australia}}</ref>

==Description==
{{multiple image
 | align     = left
 | direction = vertical
 | image1    = Cylindroputnia_imbricata.jpg
 | width1    = 185
 | caption1  = Cane cholla blossom
 | image2    = Cane cholla, with flower, Albuquerque.JPG
 | width2    = 185
 | caption2  = 
}}
The above-ground part consists of much-branched cylindrical stems, the end joints being about {{convert|3|cm|in|abbr=on}} in diameter. The joints, unlike those of some [[Cylindropuntia|chollas]], are hard to detach. The stems are highly tubercular (lumpy)<ref name=J&H>{{cite web | last = Johnson | first = F. L. | author2 = B. W. Hoagland | title = ''Opuntia imbricata'' (Haw.) DC. | work = Catalog of the Woody Plants of Oklahoma: Descriptions and Range Maps | publisher = Oklahoma Biological Survey | year = 1999 | url = http://www.biosurvey.ou.edu/shrub/opim.htm | access-date = 2006-07-17 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20060713011647/http://www.biosurvey.ou.edu/shrub/opim.htm | archive-date = 2006-07-13 }}</ref> with a pattern of long oval lumps. A typical height is about {{convert|1|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}, but exceptionally it can grow to {{convert|4.6|m|ft|abbr=on}} with a "trunk" diameter of {{convert|25|cm|in|abbr=on}}.<ref name = Elmore>{{cite book| author=Elmore, Francis H. | title=Trees and Shrubs of the Southwest Uplands | publisher=Western National Parks Association | year=1978 | isbn=0-911408-41-X}}</ref> The width is often similar to or somewhat greater than the height. The stems are armed with clusters of up to about 10 red to pink<ref name=J&H/> [[spine (botany)|spines]], which may be {{convert|3|cm|in|abbr=on}} long<ref name=J&H/> and are barbed and sharp enough to easily penetrate leather gardening gloves.<ref>{{cite web | author = Irish, Mary | title = Handle With Care (Planting Cacti) | publisher = Learn2Grow | url = http://www.learn2grow.com/gardeningguides/cactisucculents/planting/handlewithcare.aspx | access-date = 2009-08-15 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20091023053834/http://www.learn2grow.com/gardeningguides/cactisucculents/planting/handlewithcare.aspx | archive-date = 2009-10-23 }}</ref> The stems and fruits also have many spines or "[[Glochid|glochids]]" about {{convert|1|mm|in|2|abbr=on}} long<ref name=J&H/> that can detach and stick in the skin.

There are two kinds of stems or "cladodes": long plagiotropic, bearing flowers at the ends and falling off after a few years, and long orthotropic, primarily serving for support and transport and staying on the plant. Plagiotropic stems grow in a star- or crown-like pattern around a central orthotropic stem.<ref name=Kunst>{{cite thesis |type=PhD |last=Kunst |first=Carlos Roberto Guillermo |date=1990 |url=http://etd.lib.ttu.edu/theses/available/etd-03252009-31295005979926/ |title=Some autoecological aspects of Opuntia imbricata (Haw.) D.C. (cholla) |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110815203802/http://etd.lib.ttu.edu/theses/available/etd-03252009-31295005979926/ |archive-date=2011-08-15 |no-pp=yes |page=(title page) |publisher=Texas Tech University |access-date=2009-08-15}}</ref>
This species blooms in late spring or early summer. The flowers are purple or magenta, rarely rose-pink, about {{convert|5|cm|in|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=J&H/> The fruits are yellowish, tubercular like the stems,<ref name=J&H/> and shaped something like the frustum of a cone, with a hollow at the wide end where the flower fell off; they are often mistaken for flowers. The plant retains them all winter. They are dry and bland, though the [[Native Americans of the United States|Indians]] of [[Arizona]] and New Mexico are said to have eaten them.<ref name=Elmore/>

In addition to sexual reproduction, the tree cholla reproduces when stem joints fall to the ground and take root. Thus, this species spreads, and its spread is hard to control, especially where animals defecate seeds and carry stem joints stuck to their hide some distance from the parent plant. (Some cows, "cholla eaters", learn to eat cholla fruits despite the pain.) "Waves of invasion" typically occur four or five years after drought combined with [[grazing]], probably because this combination exposes soil on which the stem joints can take root.<ref name=Kunst/>

==Taxonomy==
''Cylindropuntia imbricata'' was scientifically described as ''Cereus imbricatus'' by the botanist [[Adrian Hardy Haworth]] in 1821. [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] moved it to ''[[Opuntia]]'' in 1828 and [[Joseph Paxton]] published it in ''[[Echinocactus]]'' in 1840. It was given its accepted placement in ''[[Cylindropuntia]]'' in 1930 by [[Frederik Marcus Knuth (taxonomist)|Frederik Marcus Knuth]].<ref name="POWO" />

==Ecology==
[[File:Toxostoma curvirostre in Cylindropuntia imbricata.jpg|thumb|right|[[Curve-billed thrasher]] in cover.]]
The fruits are also eaten by various wild birds and mammals, including [[pronghorn]], [[desert bighorn sheep]], and [[deer]]. The thorny plants provide escape for cover for many small animals.<ref>{{cite book | last = Lamb |  first = Samuel H. | year = 1975 | title = Woody Plants of the Southwest: A Field Guide with Descriptive Text, Drawings, Range Maps, and Photographs |quote=These fruits are also safe for human consumption, with a sweet flavour and large seeds. | publisher = Sunstone Press | page = 34 | isbn = 0-913270-50-4 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=GDqMKJeKNJYC&pg=PA34 | access-date = 2009-08-18}}</ref>

The [[Megachilidae|leafcutter bee]] ''Lithurgus apicalis'' has been observed to pollinate the flowers.<ref>{{cite journal | last = Grant | first = Verne |author2=Paul D. Hurd | year = 1979 | title = Pollination of the southwestern Opuntias  | journal = Plant Systematics and Evolution | volume = 133 | issue = 1–2 | pages = 15–28 | doi = 10.1007/BF00985876 | bibcode = 1979PSyEv.133...15G | s2cid = 42903463 }} (Subscription required.)</ref>

==Uses==
The plants are sometimes grown as [[Ornamental plant|ornamentals]].<ref name=Horticopia/> Dead stems decay to leave a hollow wooden tube with a pattern of lengthwise slits. These are sometimes used as canes or to make curios. The [[Roman Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] [[Penitentes (New Mexico)|Penitentes]] of New Mexico formerly tied fresh stems to their bare backs in [[Holy Week]] processions.<ref name=Elmore/> The [[Zuni people]] use the ''imbricata'' variety ceremonially.<ref>Stevenson, Matilda Coxe 1915 Ethnobotany of the Zuni Indians. SI-BAE Annual Report #30 (p. 95)</ref>
